justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as a recent trading level in the mid-to-upper 340s range. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 349.5 is anchored heavily on short-term momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, assuming no major overnight catalysts materialize. The slight upward tilt in the one-week estimate to 351.0 reflects a mild bullish bias consistent with broader equity market conditions and typical seasonal tendencies, while the one-month estimate of 355.0 extends that gradual drift further, incorporating a reasonable assumption that the underlying fundamental backdrop remains supportive without significant deterioration.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding nature of uncertainty over time. At one day, the range of 341 to 358 is relatively tight because intraday and overnight volatility is constrained by existing liquidity and the absence of scheduled high-impact events. By one week, the interval widens to 334–368, capturing the realistic possibility of a Federal Reserve communication, an unexpected economic data release, or a shift in risk sentiment. At one month, the range of 318–392 is intentionally wide because a full calendar month introduces earnings cycles, macroeconomic data revisions, geopolitical developments, and potential changes in interest rate expectations — all of which can meaningfully reprice equity instruments.

The specific risks that could push outcomes outside even these wider intervals include a sudden credit event or systemic financial stress that triggers a sharp risk-off move, which could push prices well below 318. On the upside, an unexpectedly dovish central bank pivot or a major positive surprise in corporate earnings or economic data could drive prices above 392. Liquidity shocks, particularly around month-end rebalancing or options expiration periods, can also produce sharp, short-lived dislocations that briefly breach stated ranges before reverting.

It is also worth noting that my estimates carry inherent model uncertainty — I do not have access to real-time market data, so my baseline level may itself be miscalibrated relative to where the instrument was actually trading at the time of the forecast. This adds a layer of epistemic uncertainty on top of the aleatory uncertainty already reflected in the intervals, meaning the true distribution of outcomes is likely somewhat wider than what I have formally stated.
